title: Appendices 1-7: investor records, dated taxation, valuation, and accounting cases

claims.text: Investigating a cluster of successful managers requires prior identification, the complete eligible population and independence analysis; a shared intellectual origin is a hypothesis, not itself a proof of skill.
Different holdings do not establish statistically independent investment outcomes. Shared exposures, selection, costs, capacity and differing reporting periods still require analysis.
Reject the inference that a large appraised discount and several holdings create essentially no risk. Value realization, governance and appraisal remain uncertain.
The tax appendices are dated historical material; neither the 1972 rules nor the update labeled 2003 can be used as current tax instructions.
Precise valuation formulas can conceal highly uncertain growth and terminal assumptions. Audit the inputs and sensitivity rather than equating mathematical precision with dependable value.
Acquisition consideration must reconcile bonds at market value, warrants, tax deductions and accounting credits; reported accretion can differ from economic value creation.
claims.anchor: amortization of the huge bond discount

claims.text: Reject assuming the unobserved or delisted members of a name-selected technology sample necessarily performed worse. Missing outcomes require investigation and cannot be assigned a convenient loss.

assimilation: Use the manager records as historically attributed evidence worth examining, with separate gross/limited-partner returns, actual intervals, reinvested distributions and comparison universes. A successful method still needs a prospective test for this Character. Retain flexible business valuation while excluding obsolete tax parameters from executable policy.
adversarial_review: Buffett's asserted prior selection and audits are source claims, not independently verified registry evidence here. Low stock overlap does not eliminate common value exposure or dependence; one of four original employees is untraced. The tables include severe 1973-74 losses for Munger and Pacific Partners, qualifying the assertion of uniformly low risk. Sequoia's gross return adds an approximate annual fee, while other tables show partner allocations; pension records mix bonds and equities and use differing survey universes. Partial years and dividend conventions differ. Price declines do not mechanically increase beta. The dollar-bill analogy assumes the very value certainty an appraisal must establish. The IBM missed opportunity qualifies rigid tangible-asset screening. Reject categorical dismissal of calculus: model assumptions and evidence determine reliability. Higher earnings multipliers need not imply a squared-earnings valuation unless a particular functional relation is assumed. An extreme IPO failure and company-name prefix sample cannot establish a general probability of technology losses. Do not import the historical public-offering, tax or accounting rules as current law.
memory_delta: Demand complete prior selection, comparable net returns, dependence analysis and accessible execution before attributing skill. Inspect valuation sensitivity and full acquisition consideration. Preserve counterexamples to rigid book-value rules, exclude dated tax rules from operations, and leave missing outcomes unknown.
reading_provenance: Read all PDF pages 488-525; visually inspected all nine Superinvestors tables, including rotated pension and Perlmeter tables, and the Aetna and technology sample tables.
